content: 1. The review authors considered the risk of bias (RoB) in individual studies when interpreting and discussing the results of the review. This is a critical step to ensure the validity of the conclusions drawn from the systematic review. 2. The review authors provided a satisfactory explanation for any observed heterogeneity in the results of the review. They discussed potential sources of variability and their implications for the findings. 3. If a quantitative synthesis was performed, the review authors conducted an adequate investigation of publication bias (e.g., small study bias) and discussed its likely impact on the results of the review. This ensures that the findings are not unduly influenced by selective reporting of studies. 4. The review authors reported any potential sources of conflict of interest, including any funding they received for conducting the review. Transparency in funding and conflicts of interest is essential to maintain the credibility of the review. 5. Shea et al. (2017) introduced AMSTAR 2, a critical appraisal tool for systematic reviews that include randomized or non-randomized studies of healthcare interventions, or both. This tool is widely used to assess the methodological quality of systematic reviews. 6. Regarding all-cause and cause-specific mortality, sedentary behavior was found to be associated with all-cause mortality among adults. The evidence was systematically reviewed, and the findings were summarized based on the quality of the included studies, the number of participants, and the certainty of the evidence. 7. Berger (2019) reviewed three prospective cohort studies with a total of 277,763 participants. The studies had serious risks of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness, but no serious imprecision. Most studies relied on self-reported sedentary behavior, and the mean follow-up time was not reported. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. 8. Del Pozo-Cruz (2018) reviewed three prospective cohort studies with 12,108 participants. There was no serious risk of bias, but serious inconsistency and imprecision were noted. All studies used accelerometers to measure sedentary time (ST), defined as <100 counts per minute. Replacing 30 minutes of sedentary time with light-intensity physical activity (LIPA) or moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) was associated with a significantly lower risk of all-cause mortality. 9. Ekelund (2018) reviewed 11 prospective cohort studies with 888,327 participants. There was no serious risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, or imprecision. A dose-response relationship was observed between sitting time and all-cause mortality. Sitting time was categorized into four groups, and the highest category (>8 hours/day) was associated with increased mortality risk compared to the lowest category (<4 hours/day). 10. Ku (2018) reviewed 19 prospective cohort studies with 1,250,482 participants. There was no serious risk of bias or imprecision, but serious inconsistency and indirectness were noted. The studies used both subjective and objective measures of sedentary time, and the cut-off points for sedentary time categories varied across studies. Longer follow-up studies showed weaker associations between sedentary time and mortality risks. 11. Ku (2019) reviewed 11 prospective cohort studies with 36,341 participants aged 65 years or older. There was no serious risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, or imprecision. All studies used accelerometers to measure sedentary time, but the definitions of sedentary time varied. Increased hazards of all-cause mortality became significant when total sedentary time exceeded approximately 9 hours/day. 12. Xu (2019) reviewed seven prospective cohort studies with 284,161 participants. All measures of sedentary time and physical activity were self-reported. A dose-response relationship was observed between sedentary activity and all-cause mortality. However, the analysis did not include all eligible cohort studies, and low-intensity physical activity (LIPA) was not accounted for. 13. Ahmad (2017) reviewed 22 studies, including one case-control study, with 655 participants. There was no serious risk of bias or inconsistency, but serious indirectness and imprecision were noted. One case-control study found a significantly higher risk of myocardial infarction (MI) among those reporting >215 minutes/day of sedentary time compared to those with lower sedentary time. 14. Wang (2018) reviewed three cross-sectional studies with 56,412 participants. There was a serious risk of bias and indirectness, but no serious inconsistency or imprecision. All studies used self-reported measures of sedentary behavior, and the categorization of sedentary behavior varied widely between studies. 15. Ahmad (2017) reviewed four studies (one prospective cohort, one case-control, and two cross-sectional) with 158,964 participants. All studies suggested that greater sedentary time was associated with a higher prevalence of diabetes. The prospective cohort study found an 84% increased risk of developing diabetes in the highest quartile of TV and sitting time. 16. The evidence on sedentary behavior and its association with cardiovascular disease (CVD) incidence, cancer incidence, and type 2 diabetes incidence was systematically reviewed. The findings varied across studies, with some showing significant associations and others reporting no clear dose-response relationships. The quality of evidence was assessed based on risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, and imprecision.
